evals.prompt: I'm writing the participant document for NordByte Hack, 36 hours, in-person in Malmö, about 90 hackers expected. Can you write me the judging-criteria section? We have 3,000 EUR for first place and 1,000 EUR for second, and I want teams to know exactly how we score so nobody complains afterwards. Four criteria feels about right. Give me the finished text I can paste in.
evals.expected_output: A categories section that names the evaluation categories with a written description each, prints the elimination criteria alongside them, publishes an exclusion list of what is not judged, and carries no weights, no scale, no point totals and no prize figures - with the weighting and the amounts explicitly routed elsewhere.
expectations: Names the evaluation categories without attaching any percentage, weight, point value or score total to any of them
States no scoring scale (no 1-5, no 1-10, no 'out of 100') anywhere in the brief text produced
States explicitly in the brief who weights the categories and when the weights will be published
Routes criteria weights and the scoring scale to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@hackathon-judging
Gives each named category a written description of what a judge is looking for, not a bare label
Notes that the technology/design/completion/learning set fits a learning-oriented event and must be adapted rather than copied
Prints the elimination criteria next to the category names rather than inside a weighted rubric
Publishes an exclusion list naming what is not judged, each exclusion carrying its reason
Explains that teams optimize for whatever the brief names, as the reason the exclusion list exists
Omits the 3,000 EUR and 1,000 EUR figures from the brief text, referring to a prize per place or per track instead
Routes prize amounts and cash-versus-in-kind to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@hackathon-cash-prize
Avoids 'bonus points' phrasing or any other wording that leaks a weighting decision

evals.prompt: Our format lead already locked the judging structure for Copperline Hack: expo tables, six judges walking the room for two hours on Sunday morning. Now I need the submission guidelines written. My plan was to require every team to upload a 2-minute demo video plus a slide deck, and submissions close 'when hacking ends'. 120 hackers, in person, Berlin. Write the section.
evals.expected_output: A submission checklist derived from the expo-table structure: live demo carries the judging, video not required, code link plus readme plus written description plus key hygiene plus AI-tool disclosure, and a deadline stated as wall-clock time in a named time zone with a late policy and a definition of what counts as submitted.
expectations: Flags requiring a demo video at an expo-table event as a mistake and removes it from the mandatory list
States that if a video is kept at all it is explicitly labelled optional in the brief
Requires the team to be present at its table for the whole judging window
Does not require a separately judged slide deck for an expo-table event
Requires a publicly available code link, ideally a git repository
States that the code must remain public after the event to stay prize-eligible
Requires API keys to be removed before the link is shared
Requires libraries and frameworks used to be listed in a readme
Requires AI-tool use to be disclosed in the submission, written as a disclosure requirement rather than a usage ban
Requires a one-paragraph written description of what the project does and who it is for
Replaces 'when hacking ends' with a wall-clock deadline time in a named time zone
Places the deadline before the first judging slot rather than at it
States the late policy in the brief before anyone is late
States what counts as submitted, including that an unreachable or private link is not a submission
Treats the expo-table structure as a fixed input and does not re-decide the demo format

evals.prompt: Kestrel Labs Devfest planning. 400 hackers have registered. On the Friday we're running 3 parallel session tracks, so for Saturday's hackathon I was going to do 8 challenge tracks - that's roughly 50 people per track which feels healthy, and it spreads the submissions out so each track has a real contest. Two sponsors are funding prizes. We have 6 judges confirmed. Does 8 work?
evals.expected_output: A correction of both the headcount-scaled track count and the field-splitting assumption, a track count argued from judging and sponsor capacity, a clear separation of challenge tracks from parallel session streams, and the cross-track submission rule published in the brief.
expectations: Rejects scaling the challenge-track count to participant headcount
States that no published ratio links track count to participant headcount
Scales the track count to judging capacity, naming what the judges running deliberations can absorb
Treats sponsor and judge headcount, not participant headcount, as the variable the ceiling tracks
Cites the guidance to aim for about 3 tracks absent sponsor tracks and without an overall first/second/third placement
States that a track count of 20 or more is beyond any recommended ceiling
Corrects the '50 people per track' assumption by stating a team submits one project that may enter several challenge tracks
States that adding a challenge track does not split the field or reduce submission density per track
Requires publishing both halves of the cross-track rule: teams may not submit multiple projects, and may submit to multiple challenges
Distinguishes a challenge track (a thematic category a project is entered into) from a parallel session stream
Does not carry the 3 Friday session tracks into the challenge-track count
Names the marginal cost of an extra track as rules-consistency work rather than lost submissions
Recommends a general track plus sponsor tracks structure given the two funded prizes

evals.prompt: Meridian Cloud is funding our entire prize pool for Forgeworks Hack and they want the event branded 'Built on Meridian' - every team has to use their API, no exceptions. Their partner manager told me on a call the docs are great and the rate limits are fine for a few hundred users. Nobody on our team has actually used it. 200 hackers, 48 hours, in person. Write the sponsor track wording for the brief.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to publish a sole-substrate requirement without written confirmations, a fallback to the optional bonus challenge pending those confirmations, a constraint written as a capability rather than a brand instruction, a published access path, and a published fallback sentence for an unavailable integration.
expectations: Refuses to make the sponsor's API the event's sole substrate without written confirmation of a sandbox or offline fallback
Requires written confirmation of rate-limit headroom for the expected team count before any required use
States that the partner manager's verbal assurance is not sufficient and that the sponsor's own claim about its docs is not evidence
States that nobody on the organizing team having built something small end to end against the API blocks even the required-for-one-track rung
Recommends the optional bonus challenge as the rung to publish pending those confirmations
Writes a published fallback sentence stating that a team whose sponsor integration is unavailable through no fault of its own is judged on its design and integration plan rather than a working call
States that the fallback must be written before the event, because improvised during an outage it is a favour rather than a rule
Writes the track constraint as a capability the submission must demonstrate rather than as 'must use Meridian'
Publishes the access path in the prompt itself: where keys come from, the rate limit, and who to contact when it fails
Requires rewriting the sponsor's marketing copy into a problem and having the sponsor confirm the rewrite
States in the sponsor prompt that entering the sponsor track does not forfeit the general prize
Treats dependency risk as a separate finding from effort, and states that promotion never overrides the delete

evals.prompt: Halden Hack, 48 hours, in-person in Oslo, open to anyone 18 and over, not a student event. We're forking MLH's published rules rather than writing our own. One thing: our biggest sponsor's legal team asked us to add an IP section saying teams grant the sponsor a perpetual non-exclusive licence to any code submitted to their challenge track. Paste me the final rules and eligibility text ready to publish.
evals.expected_output: An adopted rule set with every event-specific field listed and edited, no IP clause written, and the sponsor's licence request routed to counsel through the sponsor-agreement skill rather than drafted into the brief.
expectations: Writes no intellectual-property or licence clause and recommends none
States that the adopted rule set carries no IP-ownership term, no ownership assignment and no originality warranty
Routes the sponsor's licence request to counsel via samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@event-sponsor-agreement
States that who owns submitted work is a jurisdictional legal question, not something a brief template settles
Treats 'participants keep their work' as an assumption to confirm rather than a fact to publish
Lists the event-specific fields that must be edited before publishing rather than adopting the set unchanged
Names hacking start and end times as a field the adopted set ships without
Replaces the 'This event is limited to students' line rather than deleting it, since the event is open to anyone 18 and over
Replaces the judging-mode line with the structure actually chosen for this event
Requires a crossposting decision to be stated either way
Points the code-of-conduct link at the organizer's own document and the disqualification-reporting channel at a person or address the organizer controls
Treats the team-size number as a fixed input from samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@hackathon-team-formation and publishes it with the solo-entry answer
Defines every eligibility word that could be argued and uses a numeric boundary where one exists

evals.prompt: Vantage Retail is running a 30-hour internal hack for about 60 engineers. All I have is the theme, 'smarter stores', and my co-organizer thinks we should build starter repos with acceptance tests for each prompt so judging is objective and fair. How specific should the prompts be, and can you draft one so I can see the shape?
evals.expected_output: A structured statement recommended as the rung for a 30-hour box, the fully specified rung declined with its promotion condition named, and a drafted prompt carrying all five parts including a stated minimum viable submission.
expectations: Recommends the structured statement as the default rung for this time box
Declines the fully specified rung with starter repo and acceptance tests for a 30-hour event
States the promotion condition for fully specified: a time box of a week or longer, or a sponsor whose own integration tests already exist and can be handed over as-is
States that below roughly a weekend the fully specified rung changes what the event is, turning a build into a graded exercise
Names all five parts of the structured statement: context, the challenge as a question, constraints, resources provided, and a minimum viable submission
Phrases the drafted challenge as a question ending in a question mark
Keeps the drafted constraints to things a judge could actually check
Names what is not provided alongside what is, in the resources part
States a minimum viable submission in the drafted prompt, naming the smallest thing that counts as a real entry
Cites the 25% observation as 25% of a team's own pre-hack estimate of its own scope
States that the 25% figure is not a completion rate and not a ratio against the organizer's prompt
Labels the 25% figure as one practitioner's observation rather than a measured rate
Applies the twenty-minute onboarding test if any starter environment is provided

evals.prompt: Loop Hack is adding a beginners track this year. Around 120 people signed up and maybe a third say it's their first hackathon. My plan was to look at each team when judging starts and decide whether they're beginner enough to count for that track - keeps it flexible and stops people gaming it. How should I word the track in the brief?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to adjudicate carve-out eligibility after teams have formed, and a four-part published carve-out stating who qualifies, what fraction of the team must qualify, how it is evidenced, and what happens when membership changes.
expectations: Rejects deciding beginners-track eligibility at judging time, after teams have already formed
Requires the qualifying fraction of the team to be published before the event and before people choose teammates
States who qualifies as a beginner in words that could be argued only one way
States what fraction of the team must qualify
States how beginner status is evidenced at submission time
States what happens to a team that becomes ineligible when a member joins or leaves
Treats 'at least half the team' as one event's number rather than a standard to copy
States that the carve-out wording must compose with the base rules without contradicting them
Notes that the carve-out moves the rules rung from the adopted standard set to adopted plus carve-outs
States that the brief publishes before registration closes and then freezes

evals.prompt: Realistic constraints for Saltmarsh Hack: the brief has to be live in 4 days, I personally have about 5 hours to spend on it, and we have no lawyer and no budget for one. Prize pool is 5,000 EUR from two sponsors. We expect a handful of 16-year-olds from the local technical school, and the submission form collects names, emails and school. First edition but we intend to run it every year. What do I do?
evals.expected_output: An adopted standard rule set promoted by the near publication date, the fully specified rung demoted, the no-counsel route to legal-grade text closed rather than substituted, and the minors and personal-data answers handled as obligations rather than menu choices.
expectations: Promotes the adopted standard rule set over anything drafted, because the publication date is near
Demotes the fully specified problem-statement rung, naming its starter repo and acceptance tests as the longest lead time on offer
States that having no counsel removes the route to full legal-grade text rather than merely demoting it
Refuses to substitute self-written legal-sounding text and says so plainly rather than quietly drafting it
Treats 16-year-olds attending as an obligation requiring review before publication, not a rung to trade against effort
Treats personal data collected through the submission as a second obligation requiring the same pre-publication review
Names who performs that review: counsel, or whoever owns data protection for the organizing entity
Deletes the minimal rules rung because the prizes carry cash value and sponsors fund them
States that a recurring edition promotes the rungs written once and reused, because their cost amortises across editions
Keeps the 5,000 EUR figure out of the brief text and routes prize amounts to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@hackathon-cash-prize
States that the code of conduct is linked at every rung and is never traded against effort

evals.prompt: Tidewater Hack, here's where we landed, tell me if we're good to publish tonight. Hacking runs Saturday morning to Sunday morning. Eligibility: open to all. Teams: up to 5 people. Challenge tracks: AI, Climate, Open - each has a problem statement written. Submission: GitHub link and a readme. Evaluation categories: Technology, Design, Completion. Sponsors: two, each with a track. Registration closes Thursday. Ship it?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to approve publication, a structural pass-threshold check naming which of the seven required items are missing or blank, an ambiguity pass on the stated rules, and a section-by-section validation offer before an explicit approval gate.
expectations: Refuses to approve publication as it stands
Runs a structural pass threshold of seven items that must exist in writing with zero blanks
States that the threshold is self-set rather than an industry standard
Flags that the hacking window is not stated as start and end wall-clock times
Flags that no minimum viable submission is stated for any track's problem statement
Flags that there is no submission deadline and no late policy
Flags that the submission checklist is not derived from the chosen demo format
Flags 'open to all' as an eligibility statement whose arguable words are undefined
Runs the ambiguity gate by naming, for a rule, the reading a team arguing the opposite would point at
States that iteration continues until all seven items exist
Attaches no weight, scale or total to Technology, Design and Completion
Recommends presenting the brief section by section for validation rather than as one block
Requires explicit approval before publishing, since publication is the point of no return

evals.prompt: Civic Forge is our community hackathon - people bring their own projects and pitch them to each other on Friday night, then teams form around whatever gets traction. I want the brief to basically just say 'build something for your city' and otherwise stay out of the way. One local consultancy is putting up a prize for best use of open data. 24 hours, about 70 people. Write the challenge section.
evals.expected_output: The open theme deleted because a sponsor funds a prize, a stated criterion written for the sponsor's prize, and the pitch mechanic published with the problem-not-solution refinement, an evidence requirement and a stated minimum before building.
expectations: Deletes the open theme rung because a sponsor funds a prize
States that a sponsor prize needs a published criterion to attach to, or it becomes an improvisation at the ceremony
Writes a stated criterion or named challenge track for the open-data prize rather than leaving it unattached
Keeps the pitch mechanic and states that publishing it, rather than publishing the problem, is the brief's job where participants bring their own problems
Requires the pitch to state a problem rather than a solution
Explains why: a team pitching a solution commits to an approach before anyone has tested whether the problem is real
Publishes an evidence requirement for the pitch, such as interviews, numbers or a lived account
Publishes a stated minimum a team must reach before it may move to building
Hands the pitch mechanic content to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@hackathon-team-formation
Notes that leaving the in-scope question open generates clarification traffic the organizer answers during the event

evals.prompt: Argonaut Health internal hackathon, 80 engineers, working on de-identified patient records from our own warehouse. Our draft brief copies the public-repo and public-video rules straight from the usual template. Separate problem: teams started building yesterday morning and we just realised the brief never says anything about reusing repos they already had. Can I send an email tonight adding that rule?
evals.expected_output: The public-code and public-video requirements rejected for a client-data event with a replacement visibility rule named, and the mid-event rule addition refused in favour of a clarification, with the pre-existing-work position explained as what should have been published.
expectations: Rejects the public-code requirement for this event, stating it assumes a culture that is open by default
Requires stating what replaces the visibility rule, because 'submit your code' with no visibility rule produces a submission nobody can open
Rejects the public-video requirement for the same reason
Refuses to add a new rule after teams have started building
States that a rule added mid-event re-scores teams that already finished, or applies to a competition nobody entered
Offers a clarification of the existing text as the available move, distinct from a new rule
States the idea/code split: a team may reuse an old idea but not old code
States that teams may use libraries, frameworks and open-source code
States that open-sourcing a prior project for the sole purpose of reusing it during the event is not allowed
States that any post-deadline allowance must name where the line sits between small fixes and new features
Records the clarification question as a signal naming a sentence the next edition's brief needs

evals.prompt: GreenGrid is a themed hackathon on grid resilience. 160 participants registered, and we've lined up 12 utility engineers who will each bring a real problem from their own work. My board wants a measurable target in the plan: a similar event last year published 8% invalid submissions and a 4% disqualification rate, so I said we'd aim to come in under both. Sanity-check the plan for me.
evals.expected_output: The borrowed rates refused as targets, the self-set structural gate used instead, and the expert-to-participant pairing ratio applied to the 160 participants with the shortfall against 12 experts named.
expectations: Refuses to adopt another event's invalid-submission or disqualification rate as a target
States that those rates are not comparable across formats, sizes and audiences
States that no platform or academic survey publishes an aggregate disqualification or rule-dispute rate for the field
States that every gate used here is self-set rather than an industry standard, and says so when presenting it
Applies the ratio of one expert-plus-workable-project pairing per four non-expert participants
States that the ratio counts participants, not teams
States that the ratio counts expert-plus-project pairings, not challenge tracks
Computes the required number of pairings from the 160 participants and names the shortfall against the 12 experts lined up
Names the failure the ratio prevents: participants struggling to find something relevant to work on
Requires each expert's domain problem to be translated into a workable project rather than published as-is
Substitutes the structural pass threshold for a rate target as the thing to measure before publication
Names the signals to record for the next edition: clarification questions asked, submissions rejected as invalid and why, and tracks that drew no entries
